kurals.tamil:
பெண்ணியலார் எல்லாரும் கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்
நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Penniyalaar ellaarum kannin podhu-unpar
nannen paraththa-nin maarpu
kurals.meaning: Wanderer, every woman feasts her eyes on your broad chest as if it belonged to all; so I will not come near it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your favourite teddy bear being passed around the whole class until it no longer feels like yours. A wife in this poem playfully tells her husband that since everyone admires him, she will pretend she does not want to sit close to him.
kurals.university: The chapter title pulavi nuṇukkam means ‘the fine points (nuṇukkam) of love-sulking (pulavi)’: in the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, Valluvar sketches how a loving wife turns the smallest innocent word or act of her husband into a pretext for a mock quarrel, and Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes this first couplet as the wife’s own speech. She addresses him as paratta (‘man of wandering ways’) and says that all of feminine nature (peṇ-iyalār) ‘eat’ his chest with their eyes as a common possession (potu uṇpar), so she will not approach (naṇṇēn) it. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read the eye-feasting literally as other women’s admiring glances, while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it into a charge that he is ‘shared’ with women of the street; Pope renders it ‘From thy regard all womankind enjoys an equal grace; O thou of wandering fickle mind, I shrink from thine embrace.’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the eighth canto of Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Krishna comes to Radha at dawn still showing the signs of a night spent with another cowherd girl, and Radha, cast as the wounded heroine (khandita), sends him away with bitter teasing: go to the one you were with.
hinduism.explanation: Radha’s anger is the classic Sanskrit picture of a beloved who refuses an embrace because her lover has been shared with others.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Radha, the Kural’s wife declares she will not come near a chest that, in her playful accusation, belongs to every woman.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a strong match on the jealous refusal, though Radha’s grievance is real while the Kural’s wife is largely feigning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that in marriage each spouse belongs to the other, so neither is a common possession.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s complaint rests on the same idea: her husband should be hers, not shared by every admiring eye.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a fair match on mutual belonging, though Paul gives a rule for marriage, not a lover’s teasing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers, with a parallel command for women in the next verse, to lower their gaze rather than feast their eyes on others.
islam.tie_back: The wife objects to exactly the kind of looking the verse forbids: other women feasting their eyes on her husband.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a real teaching on the wandering gaze, but it is a moral command, not a wife’s mock jealousy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously, though she is thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.”
judaism.explanation: Malachi rebukes husbands who betray the wife of their youth and reminds them that she is their covenant partner.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife voices, in play, the same claim Malachi makes in earnest: a husband owes himself to his own wife.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a solid match on marital loyalty, though the prophet speaks of real betrayal, not a lovers’ game.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha lists the ways a husband should care for his wife, including by honouring her, not despising her, and not being unfaithful to her.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist lay ethics make faithfulness one of a husband’s plain duties to his wife.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s teasing charge of ‘wandering’ presumes this same duty of faithfulness.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested list of a husband’s duties; a reasonable match on fidelity, though the sutta is prescriptive and has no sulking.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Haṭha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: The nun Rajimati rebukes Rathanemi, warning that a heart which goes after every woman it sees has no anchor.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife teases her husband as a ‘wanderer’ whose chest belongs to everyone, the same rootless love Rajimati condemns.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a good match on the wandering heart, though Rajimati speaks to a monk tempted to break his vows, not to a husband.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, the goddess Calypso offers Odysseus immortality if he stays with her, but he tells her that, though Penelope cannot match her beauty, he still longs every day to go home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus keeps his heart for his own wife even when another, more dazzling partner wants him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife wants exactly this: a husband who belongs to her, not to every woman who admires him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a fair match on exclusive devotion, but it shows the husband’s faithfulness rather than a wife’s teasing jealousy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Pausanias distinguishes a ‘common’ (Pandemos) love, which attaches to anyone and loves the body more than the soul, from a ‘heavenly’ love that is faithful and lasting.
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias contrasts love that belongs to everyone and no one with love that is constant to one person.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s word potu (‘common’) makes the same contrast: she refuses a chest she pretends has become common property.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known speech; a good conceptual match on ‘common’ versus faithful love, though Plato’s setting is philosophical, not domestic.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடி இருந்தேமாத் தும்மினார் யாம்தம்மை
நீடுவாழ் கென்பாக் கறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ooti irundhaemaath thumminaar yaamdhammai
neetuvaazh kenpaak karindhu
kurals.meaning: While I sat sulking, he sneezed, knowing I would have to break my silence and wish him ‘Long life!’
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are not talking to your brother after a squabble, and he pretends to sneeze so that you will say ‘Bless you!’ without thinking. Now you have spoken, and the game is over. That is the clever trick the husband plays here.
kurals.university: This couplet is the wife’s speech (talaivi kūṟṟu): ūṭi iruntēmā means ‘as we were sulking’, and she reports that he sneezed (tummiṉār) knowing (aṟintu) that we would say nīṭu vāḻka (‘live long’) to him. It rests on the old Tamil custom of blessing a person who sneezes, which forces the sulking wife to speak and so end her silence. Solomon Pappaiah adds that he sneezed deliberately and that she, despite herself, did bless him; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it the same way. Pope renders it ‘One day we silent sulked; he sneezed: the reason well I knew; he thought that I, to speak well pleased, would say, “Long life to you!”’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the ninth canto of the Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend urges her to drop her proud sulk (mana) toward Krishna, who is eager to make up, telling her not to be proud with Madhava.
hinduism.explanation: Sanskrit love poetry treats the beloved’s sulk as something that must eventually be coaxed into giving way.
hinduism.tie_back: The husband’s sneeze is his own trick for making the sulking wife give way and speak.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the canto’s refrain; a reasonable match on breaking a lover’s sulk, though there is no sneeze or blessing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.”
christianity.explanation: When Elisha revives the Shunammite’s son, the child’s sneezing is the first sign that life has returned.
christianity.tie_back: The sneeze in the Kural also signals life, which is why custom answers it with a wish for long life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); only a next-best link through the sneeze as a sign of life, with nothing about love or sulking.

islam.quote_or_event: “If anyone of you sneezes, he should say ‘Al-Hamduli l-lah’ (Praise be to Allah), and his (Muslim) brother or companion should say to him, ‘Yar-hamuka-l-lah’ (May Allah bestow his Mercy on you).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes answering a sneeze with a blessing a duty of companionship.
islam.tie_back: The husband counts on just such a duty: a sneeze obliges the person beside you to bless you, even mid-quarrel.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a close match on the custom of blessing a sneezer, though the hadith is general etiquette, not a love scene.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The members of the house of Rabban Gamliel would not say good health when someone sneezed in the study hall, due to the fact that it would lead to suspension of study in the study hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud takes for granted that people wish ‘good health’ (marpe) to someone who sneezes, noting only one setting where it was skipped.
judaism.tie_back: The husband relies on the same reflex: a sneeze draws out a wish for health, here the Tamil ‘Live long!’.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 53a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Koren-Steinsaltz English); a genuine parallel on the sneeze-blessing custom, with no lovers’ quarrel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vinaya, when the Buddha sneezed while teaching, the monks called out ‘Long life to you, Lord!’; he asked whether such a wish could make anyone live or die and forbade monks to say it, but later allowed them to answer laypeople who wished them long life.
buddhism.explanation: The story records the same custom of answering a sneeze with ‘long life’, and the Buddha’s cool view of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s whole joke depends on this very custom of wishing long life to someone who sneezes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Vinaya passage; a strong match on the long-life sneeze blessing, though it concerns monastic rules, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an impassioned deer allured (by a song) rushes into death, without being satisfied with the sound.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching warns that the ear, like the eye, can be used to lure a being toward what it longs for.
jainism.tie_back: The husband’s sneeze is a sound used as a lure, drawing his wife out of her silence before she can stop herself.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a next-best match on sound as a lure, but the Jain verse warns against sense-attachment while the Kural is a playful domestic scene.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, as Penelope speaks of the hoped-for return of Odysseus, Telemachus sneezes loudly so that the hall rings, and Penelope laughs and takes the sneeze as a good omen for her words.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Homer’s Greeks, a sneeze at a meaningful moment was a sign worth answering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In the Kural too, a well-timed sneeze carries meaning and demands a response from the woman who hears it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene; a good match on the sneeze as a meaningful sign, though it is an omen, not a lover’s trick.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Aristotelian Problems asks why people regard a sneeze as sacred or divine while they do not treat a cough that way, and tries to explain the custom.
philosophy.explanation: Greek natural philosophy noticed that sneezes, unlike other bodily noises, were greeted with reverence and good wishes.
philosophy.tie_back: The husband exploits exactly this special status of the sneeze, which compels a blessing.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from a work of the Aristotelian school; a next-best match on the custom behind the couplet, with no love theme.

kurals.tamil:
கோட்டுப்பூச் சூடினும் காயும் ஒருத்தியைக்
காட்டிய சூடினீர் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Koattup-pooch chootinum kaayum oruththiyaik
kaattiya sootineer endru
kurals.meaning: Even if I wear a garland of flowers from the branches, she is angry and says I put them on to show off to some other woman.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you wear a new cap to school and your best friend frowns, ‘Who are you trying to impress?’ You only wanted to look nice! The husband here wears flowers and his wife pretends he must be dressing up for someone else.
kurals.university: From here the speaker is generally taken to be the husband, reporting the ‘fine points’ of his wife’s sulking. Kōṭṭuppū means flowers that bloom on tree branches (kōṭu), as opposed to creeper or water flowers; even if he wears (cūṭiṉum) such a garland, she grows hot with anger (kāyum), saying ‘you wore them to show (kāṭṭiya) to some woman (oruttiyai)’. Puliyur Kesikan reads the line as the husband putting the flowers on her, while Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take him to be wearing them himself; Pope follows the latter: ‘She cries, “Pray, for what woman now do you put on your flowers?”’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Harivamsa and later retellings, Krishna gives a blossom of the heavenly Parijata tree to Rukmini, and Satyabhama, hurt that the flower went to another wife, sulks until Krishna promises to bring her the whole tree.
hinduism.explanation: The story makes a single flower the trigger for a queen’s jealous, sulking anger.
hinduism.tie_back: In the Kural, too, a garland of flowers is enough to make the wife suspect another woman.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode whose details vary between the Harivamsa, Vishnu Purana 5.30 and popular versions; a strong match on flowers sparking jealousy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs admits that love brings jealousy with it, burning as fiercely as love itself.
christianity.tie_back: The wife’s quick flare of jealousy over a garland is a small spark of the fire this verse describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on love-born jealousy, though the Song’s tone is grave rather than playful.

islam.quote_or_event: When one of the Prophet’s wives sent a dish of food to the house where he was staying, the wife of that house struck the servant’s hand so the dish broke; the Prophet gathered the pieces and said, “Your mother (my wife) felt jealous,” and replaced the dish.
islam.explanation: The Prophet met a wife’s sudden jealousy with gentle understanding instead of anger.
islam.tie_back: Like that broken dish, the garland in the Kural is an innocent object that jealousy turns into a grievance.
islam._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase with the Prophet’s words quoted from sunnah.com; a good match on jealousy over a small object, though the jealousy there is between co-wives.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wrath is cruel, and anger is overwhelming; but who is able to stand before jealousy?”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ranks jealousy as harder to withstand than plain anger.
judaism.tie_back: The husband finds that no innocent explanation of his flowers can stand before his wife’s jealousy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a good match on jealousy’s force, though the proverb is general wisdom, not a love scene.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that fondness for someone breeds fear of losing them.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s fear that the flowers are meant for another woman grows out of her very fondness for her husband.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a partial match explaining jealous fear, though the Buddha counsels letting go of attachment rather than enjoying love’s quarrels.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you owned the beauty of Vaiśramaṇa, the pleasing manners of Nalakūbara, if you were like Purandara himself, I should have no desire for you.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati tells the would-be lover Rathanemi that no amount of beauty or charm will win her.
jainism.tie_back: The husband’s adornment likewise fails to soften his wife, who reads his flowers as a fault rather than a charm.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a next-best match on adornment failing to please, but Rajimati’s refusal is a nun’s firm virtue, not a wife’s feigned jealousy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ Women of Trachis, Deianira, afraid that Heracles has come to love the captive Iole, sends him a robe to win back his love, not knowing it is poisoned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tragedy shows how a wife’s jealous fear, centred on clothing and adornment, can spiral out of control.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s scene is the gentle, comic version: an adornment provokes a wife’s suspicion of another woman.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play’s plot; a partial match on jealousy tied to adornment, but the tragedy is grim where the Kural is playful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines jealousy as hatred toward a loved object joined with envy of a rival, arising when we imagine the one we love being bound to another as closely as to us.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, jealousy begins in imagination: we picture the beloved united with someone else.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife imagines her husband dressing up for another woman, exactly the imagined rival Spinoza describes.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Prop. 35 and Scholium (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Spinoza’s definition; a good conceptual match on imagined rivals, though Spinoza analyses a passion the Kural treats lightly.

kurals.tamil:
யாரினும் காதலம் என்றேனா ஊடினாள்
யாரினும் யாரினும் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaarinum kaadhalam endraenaa ootinaal
yaarinum yaarinum endru
kurals.meaning: When I said, ‘We love each other more than anyone,’ she sulked, demanding, ‘More than whom? More than whom?’
kurals.elementary: If you tell your friend, ‘You are my best friend, better than all the others,’ a cheeky friend might reply, ‘Which others? Who else is on your list?’ The wife turns her husband’s compliment into a question to tease him.
kurals.university: Yāriṉum kātalam means ‘we are lovers beyond anyone’; the husband meant it as the highest praise, but she seizes on yāriṉum (‘than anyone’) as if it implied a list of other women he loves less, and repeats yāriṉum yāriṉum (‘than whom? than whom?’). Solomon Pappaiah spells out her reading: she took him to mean that he loves many and her the most. The humour depends on the comparative form, which presupposes rivals; Kalaignar notes that she ‘misread a natural remark’. Pope renders it ‘“I love you more than all beside,” ’t was thus I gently spoke; “What all, what all?” she instant cried; and all her anger woke.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Narada visits Krishna’s palaces in Dvaraka and finds him in each queen’s house at the same moment, wholly present with every one of them.
hinduism.explanation: The story imagines a love so complete that no wife is loved ‘more’ or ‘less’ than another.
hinduism.tie_back: It answers the wife’s teasing ‘more than whom?’ by picturing a love that needs no comparison at all.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; an indirect match on comparison in love, and its divine setting differs from a single human marriage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as slow to take offence and unwilling to read bad meaning into what it hears.
christianity.tie_back: The wife does the opposite in play: she reads a hidden rival into her husband’s loving words.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a contrast rather than a parallel, since Paul describes love that does not take offence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And you will never be able to be equal [in feeling] between wives, even if you should strive [to do so]. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave another hanging.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an admits frankly that love cannot be measured out equally between people.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s ‘more than whom?’ seizes on this very idea that love can be ranked between rivals.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a partial match on comparing love, though the verse regulates plural marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he went in also unto Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah.”
judaism.explanation: Genesis records Jacob’s love in comparative terms, and the rivalry between the two sisters follows directly from it.
judaism.tie_back: The husband’s ‘more than anyone’ sounds to his wife like Jacob’s ‘more than Leah’, a love that implies a rival.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a good match on love stated as a comparison, though the Kural’s rivals are imaginary.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who seeks another’s faults, who is ever censorious — his cankers grow. He is far from destruction of the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that a mind bent on finding fault keeps feeding its own unrest.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife hunts for a fault in a compliment, though here the fault-finding is a loving game.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; only a partial match, since the verse condemns real fault-finding and the Kural’s is play.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is very fond of a lovely ‘colour,’ hates all others; hence a fool will suffer misery, but a dispassionate sage is not affected by it.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching observes that strong attachment to one thing breeds aversion to everything compared with it.
jainism.tie_back: The wife hears ‘more than anyone’ as a ranking that sets her against unseen others, the comparing mind this verse describes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a next-best match on attachment and comparison, framed as a warning against attachment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Zeus tells Hera that desire has never overcome him as it does now, not even for the wife of Ixion, nor Danae, nor Europa, nor Semele, nor Alcmene, nor Demeter, nor Leto, nor Hera herself before.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus tries to flatter Hera by comparing his love for her with a long list of other loves, comically naming the very rivals she resents.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s joke made explicit: loving someone ‘more than anyone’ invites the question ‘which others?’
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous catalogue; a near-exact match on a comparative compliment that names rivals, though Zeus’s rivals are real.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by their judgements about things.
philosophy.explanation: A word or event becomes upsetting only through the meaning we give it.
philosophy.tie_back: The husband’s compliment upsets the wife only because of the meaning she chooses to read into it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim; a good fit on interpretation causing upset, though Epictetus has no love setting.

kurals.tamil:
இம்மைப் பிறப்பில் பிரியலம் என்றேனாக்
கண்நிறை நீர்கொண் டனள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Immaip pirappil piriyalam endraenaak
kannirai neerkon danal
kurals.meaning: When I said, ‘In this life we shall never part,’ her eyes filled with tears, as if I meant we would part in the next.
kurals.elementary: Imagine telling your grandmother, ‘I will visit you every day this summer!’ and she asks, sadly, ‘Only this summer?’ The wife hears ‘in this life’ and worries it means ‘not in the next one’.
kurals.university: Immaip piṟappil means ‘in this present birth’ and piriyalam ‘we shall not part’; the wife takes the limiting phrase to imply that in a later birth (maṟumai) they will part, and her eyes fill (kaṇ niṟai nīr koṇṭaṉaḷ). The couplet assumes the belief in rebirth shared by the Tamil tradition and depends on the idea that true lovers should remain together across births. Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it this way, while Kalaignar has her ask, more sceptically, whether there is a next birth at all. Pope: ‘“While here I live, I leave you not,” I said to calm her fears. She cried, “There, then, I read your thought”; and straight dissolved in tears.’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, when Yama comes to take the soul of Satyavan, his wife Savitri follows the god of death and, through her steadfast devotion and wisdom, wins her husband back from him.
hinduism.explanation: Savitri refuses to let even death part her from her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife in the Kural weeps because she wants exactly what Savitri won: a union that does not end with this life.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya (Savitri story) (tr. K.M. Ganguli; paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous story; a strong match on love outlasting death, though Savitri wins back this life rather than a future birth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that marriage as we know it belongs to this age and does not continue in the same form after the resurrection.
christianity.tie_back: This is the very thought that makes the Kural’s wife weep: that the bond of this life might not carry into the next.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a contrastive parallel on whether marriage outlasts this life, from a very different theology.

islam.quote_or_event: “Gardens of perpetual residence; they will enter them with whoever were righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises that righteous spouses will be reunited in Paradise.
islam.tie_back: It offers the hope the Kural’s wife longs for: that husband and wife will not be parted after this life.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a good match on union beyond death, though Islam speaks of resurrection, not rebirth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Concerning anyone who divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears about him.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the parting of husband and wife is so grievous that even the altar weeps.
judaism.tie_back: The wife’s tears at the mere thought of a future parting echo this rabbinic sense that separation of spouses calls for weeping.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 22a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Koren-Steinsaltz English); a fair match on tears over separation, though the Talmud speaks of divorce, not rebirth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “We want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come.”
buddhism.explanation: Nakula’s parents tell the Buddha they wish to be together in future lives, and he explains that spouses matched in faith, virtue, generosity and discernment will meet again.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural wife’s wish: not only this life together, but the next one too.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a near one-to-one match on spouses hoping to stay together across lives.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Râgîmatî thought: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.’”
jainism.explanation: When Neminatha renounced the world on his wedding day, his bride Rajimati was overwhelmed with grief at being parted from him, and then followed him into the ascetic life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife weeps at the mere thought of a parting; Rajimati lived that parting and met it by following her beloved on the same path.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a partial match on grief at separation, though Jain tradition turns it toward renunciation, not continued married love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, the old couple Baucis and Philemon ask the gods that they may die at the same hour so neither must see the other’s grave, and they are turned together into an oak and a linden.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their one wish is never to be parted, not even by death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife weeps because she wants the same thing: a love that no life or death divides.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous tale; a strong match on wishing never to be parted, though it ends in transformation, not rebirth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes imagines Hephaestus offering two lovers to weld them into one, so that they live as one and, when they die, remain one even in Hades.
philosophy.explanation: Aristophanes’ myth says lovers long to be united not only in life but beyond it.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s tears express the same longing: she will not settle for a union that ends with this life.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous speech; a strong match on lovers wishing to stay one even after death.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளினேன் என்றேன்மற் றென்மறந்தீர் என்றென்னைப்
புல்லாள் புலத்தக் கனள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullinaen endraen-mat ren-marandheer endrennaip
pullaal pulaththak kanal
kurals.meaning: When I said, ‘I thought of you,’ she asked, ‘So you had forgotten me?’ and, instead of embracing me, began to sulk.
kurals.elementary: If you tell your friend, ‘I remembered you today!’ a teasing friend might say, ‘Only today? So you forgot me yesterday?’ The wife plays the same word game with her husband.
kurals.university: Uḷḷiṉēṉ means ‘I recalled (you)’; the wife argues, as Mu. Varadarasanar puts it, that recalling presupposes forgetting (niṉaippukku muṉ maṟappu uṇṭu), so she asks eṉ maṟantīr (‘why did you forget?’), and, though about to embrace him (pullāḷ, ‘she did not embrace’), turns to sulking (pulattakkaṉaḷ). The logic is the same as in 1314: a loving word is pressed for an implication it never had. Solomon Pappaiah notes that she had begun to embrace him and stopped; Pope: ‘“Each day I called to mind your charms,” “O, then, you had forgot,” she cried, and then her opened arms, forthwith embraced me not.’ The line division reads மற் றென்மறந்தீர் on both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Shakuntala, King Dushyanta, under a curse, forgets his wife Shakuntala, and only the sight of the ring he gave her brings his memory and grief back.
hinduism.explanation: The drama turns on the anguish of a beloved who has been forgotten and the joy of being remembered again.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife treats even a passing lapse of memory as a small version of Shakuntala’s wound.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play’s central plot; a good match on forgetting a beloved, though Dushyanta’s forgetting is real and cursed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.”
christianity.explanation: God promises a love that never forgets, even more constant than a mother’s.
christianity.tie_back: The wife demands this kind of never-forgetting love, so that ‘I remembered you’ already sounds like a confession of forgetting.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on love that never forgets, though it is God’s love for Israel.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me… When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’” Aisha replied, “by Allah, O Allah’s Messenger, I leave nothing but your name.”
islam.explanation: Aisha’s anger at the Prophet only went as far as leaving out his name, while her love stayed whole.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise withholds only her embrace for a moment, while her love remains underneath the sulk.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a strong match on a wife’s small, surface-level anger within deep affection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: In the Song of Songs, the beloved hesitates to open the door, and by the time she does, her lover has gone.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Song, a moment of holding back between lovers, here the wife’s withheld embrace, interrupts their meeting.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a partial match on a delayed embrace, though the Song’s delay is not a word game about memory.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who harbor such thoughts do not still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that dwelling on supposed slights keeps resentment alive.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife holds onto an imagined slight, ‘you forgot me’, and so keeps the sulk going, though only in play.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a next-best match, since the verse is about real hatred and the Kural’s grievance is playful.

jainism.quote_or_event: Mahavira’s teaching tells the ascetic not to watch the beauty, laughter and glances of women nor to keep a recollection of them in his mind.
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monk, deliberately not remembering the beloved is part of the discipline of chastity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s scene runs the other way: for the loving wife, any gap in remembering is itself an offence.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verse read on sacred-texts.com; a contrastive, next-best link only, since Jain monastic teaching sets aside the remembrance that married love demands.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus finally returns, Penelope holds back from embracing him until he proves himself by the secret of their bed built around an olive tree; only then does she run to him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope deliberately withholds her embrace, testing her husband before she yields.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise stops short of embracing her husband, holding back to test him with her question.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a good match on a wife’s withheld embrace, though Penelope’s caution is serious, not playful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle lists among the things that make people angry being slighted by those who forget us, even forgetting our names, because forgetting seems a sign that we do not matter to them.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees forgetting as a form of slight that naturally provokes anger.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s mock anger works on the same logic: if he had to ‘remember’ her, he must once have forgotten.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong conceptual match on forgetting as a slight.

kurals.tamil:
வழுத்தினாள் தும்மினேன் ஆக அழித்தழுதாள்
யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Vazhuththinaal thumminen aaka azhiththazhudhaal
yaarullith thummineer endru
kurals.meaning: When I sneezed, she blessed me, then took it back and wept, asking, ‘Who was thinking of you, that you sneezed?’
kurals.elementary: Some people say that when you sneeze, someone somewhere is thinking about you. Here the wife first says ‘Bless you!’, then suddenly cries, ‘Wait, who was thinking about you?’
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a second Tamil belief about sneezing: that one sneezes when someone is thinking of (uḷḷi) one. She first blesses him (vaḻuttiṉāḷ), as custom requires, then cancels it (aḻittu) and weeps (aḻutāḷ), asking yār uḷḷit tummiṉīr (‘thinking of whom did you sneeze?’, or ‘at whose thought’). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss the blessing as the wish of ‘a hundred years’ (nūṟāṇṭu). Pope: ‘She hailed me when I sneezed one day; but straight with anger seized, she cried; “Who was the woman, pray, thinking of whom you sneezed?”’ The text matches on ytamizh.com (which omits the closing full stop) and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on something breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, thwarted desire breeds anger, and anger clouds judgement and memory.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes how quickly a loving mind can slide into anger and confusion.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife’s swift slide from blessing to suspicious tears is a small, comic instance of that chain.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known verses; a partial, psychological match only, as the Gita warns against attachment rather than describing lovers’ play.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.”
christianity.explanation: James notes how the same mouth can bless and then turn to reproach.
christianity.tie_back: The wife does just that: her mouth blesses her husband and, a moment later, accuses him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on blessing turning to reproach, though James condemns it morally.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against building suspicion on mere guesses about others.
islam.tie_back: The wife builds a whole rival out of one sneeze, the kind of guesswork the verse warns against, though in playful form.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a contrastive match on groundless suspicion, from a moral command rather than a love poem.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches giving others the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.tie_back: The wife does the reverse in jest, weighting the scale against her husband over a simple sneeze.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (Kulp); a contrastive match on judging favourably, with no love setting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that what we experience is shaped first by the mind that meets it.
buddhism.tie_back: A sneeze is just a sneeze; it is the wife’s loving, anxious mind that turns it into a sign of a rival.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a partial match on the mind shaping events, from a moral rather than romantic context.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching holds that our passions come not from things themselves but from the love or aversion we bring to them.
jainism.tie_back: The sneeze itself is neutral; the wife’s love turns it, in an instant, from a cause for blessing into a cause for tears.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a good psychological match, though the Jain aim is to be free of such passions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, Procris hears that her husband Cephalus, resting after the hunt, keeps calling to ‘Aura’; she takes the word for a woman’s name, though he is only calling to the cooling breeze, and her jealous mistake ends in tragedy.
greek_mythology.explanation: A harmless word, misheard as the name of a rival, sets off a wife’s jealous grief.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife does the same with a harmless sneeze, hearing in it the thoughts of another woman.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous tale; a close match on jealousy built on a misread innocent sign, though Ovid’s ending is tragic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza describes ‘vacillation of mind’ as the state in which we are moved by contrary feelings, such as love and hatred, toward the same object at once.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, the mind can be pulled by opposite emotions toward one person in the same moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s blessing and her tears, toward the same husband in the same breath, are a lively picture of such vacillation.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Prop. 17 and Scholium (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Spinoza’s account; a good conceptual match on contrary feelings toward a loved one.

kurals.tamil:
தும்முச் செறுப்ப அழுதாள் நுமர்உள்ளல்
எம்மை மறைத்திரோ என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thummuch cheruppa azhudhaal numar-ullal
emmai maraiththiroa endru
kurals.meaning: So I held back my sneeze, and she wept, saying, ‘Are you hiding from me that your own people are thinking of you?’
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are told off for sneezing, so next time you hold it in, and then you get told off for hiding it! The poor husband cannot win: sneeze or no sneeze, his wife finds something to pretend-cry about.
kurals.university: This couplet is the sequel to 1317: afraid of another quarrel, he suppresses (ceṟuppa) his sneeze (tummu), and she weeps, asking whether he is hiding from us (emmai maṟaittirō) the thought of him held by ‘your people’ (numar uḷḷal). Numar (‘your own ones’) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘those dear to you’ and by Solomon Pappaiah as ‘someone you care for’, a veiled hint at another woman. The two couplets together show the ‘subtlety’ of pulavi: every possible response becomes an occasion for sulking. Pope: ‘And so next time I checked my sneeze; she forthwith wept and cried, (that woman difficult to please), “Your thoughts from me you hide.”’ The wording is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, during the rasa dance, Krishna vanishes from the cowherd girls, and they search the forest in anguish, suspecting he has gone off with one favoured companion.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis’ grief springs from a beloved who has hidden himself and from their guess about whom he is with.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife weeps because she thinks her husband is hiding something, and imagines who might be behind it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; a partial match on suspicion of a hidden rival, set in devotional rather than domestic love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what is hidden will come to light.
christianity.tie_back: The wife assumes the same: whatever her husband hides, even a sneeze, must conceal something waiting to come out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a next-best match on suspicion of the hidden, from a very different context of judgement.

islam.quote_or_event: Aisha said that she was never as jealous of any of the Prophet’s wives as she was of Khadija, because the Prophet used to remember and praise her so often.
islam.explanation: Aisha’s jealousy was stirred not by any rival present, but by someone held in her husband’s memory.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is jealous in the same way, of whoever might be holding her husband in their thoughts.
islam._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of a hadith verified on sunnah.com; a strong match on jealousy aroused by remembrance, though there the remembering is the husband’s.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is open rebuke than love that is hidden.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs prizes openness, even when it stings, over feelings that are kept concealed.
judaism.tie_back: The wife’s complaint is exactly that her husband is hiding something; she would rather have it out in the open.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a good match on preferring openness to hidden love, though the proverb concerns friendship.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Easily seen is the fault of others, but one’s own fault is difficult to see. Like chaff one winnows another’s faults, but hides one’s own, even as a crafty fowler hides behind sham branches.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes how quickly we suspect hidden faults in others while overlooking our own.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife imagines her husband hiding behind his held-back sneeze like the fowler behind his branches.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a partial match on suspicion of hiding, as the verse is about self-examination.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that anger destroys love, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, and greed destroys everything.
jainism.explanation: Among the four passions (kashayas), deceit (maya) is singled out as what ruins friendship and trust.
jainism.tie_back: The wife treats her husband’s held-back sneeze as a small deceit, the very thing Jain teaching says erodes intimacy.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested verse (wording varies across translations, so not quoted); a partial match on concealment harming love, though the Kural’s ‘deceit’ is imaginary.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, after seeing Thetis plead with Zeus, Hera reproaches him: it is always his pleasure, she says, to plan and decide things in secret, apart from her, and never to tell her his mind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hera’s complaint is not about what Zeus did but about what he kept from her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife makes the same charge over a stifled sneeze: you are hiding your thoughts from me.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a strong match on a wife accusing her husband of hidden thoughts, though Hera’s suspicion has some ground.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld writes that jealousy feeds on doubt, turning into fury or ending as soon as doubt gives way to certainty.
philosophy.explanation: Jealousy, he notes, lives on what is uncertain or hidden.
philosophy.tie_back: The husband’s hidden sneeze gives his wife exactly the doubt on which her playful jealousy feeds.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim (numbering may differ by edition); a good match on jealousy feeding on concealment.

kurals.tamil:
தன்னை உணர்த்தினும் காயும் பிறர்க்கும்நீர்
இந்நீரர் ஆகுதிர் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannai unarththinum kaayum pirarkkum-neer
inneerar aakudhir endru
kurals.meaning: Even when I soothe her out of her sulk, she grows angry again, saying, ‘So this is how you charm other women too!’
kurals.elementary: Imagine you finally cheer up a grumpy friend with a funny joke, and she says, ‘Hmph, I bet you tell that joke to everyone!’ Even making up becomes a new reason to tease.
kurals.university: Taṉṉai uṇarttiṉum means ‘even if I appease her (end her sulk)’; uṇarttal is the technical term for coaxing a lover out of ūṭal. Yet she grows angry (kāyum), saying piṟarkkum nīr innīrar ākutir (‘you must be like this with others too’). Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah agree on this reading, and Kalaignar adds that the husband had humbled himself to win her back. The couplet shows pulavi feeding on its own remedy, the reconciliation itself becoming fresh evidence; Pope: ‘I then began to soothe and coax, to calm her jealous mind; “I see,” quoth she, “to other folks how you are wondrous kind.”’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth canto of the Gita Govinda, Krishna pleads with the angry Radha with tender flattery, begging her to set her foot upon his head as a sign of forgiveness.
hinduism.explanation: Indian love poetry made the lover’s coaxing of a sulking beloved into an art of its own.
hinduism.tie_back: The husband here is doing the same coaxing, but his wife turns even his skill at it into a new charge.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous canto; a strong match on appeasing a sulking beloved, though Radha is eventually won over.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as willing to believe and bear with the other.
christianity.tie_back: The wife plays at refusing to believe even her husband’s reconciliation, the opposite of love that ‘believeth all things’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a contrastive match only, since Paul describes love free of suspicion.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an counsels husband and wife to settle their differences, declaring reconciliation the better way.
islam.tie_back: The husband offers just such a settlement, and the wife’s refusal to accept it is the comic heart of the couplet.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a fair match on reconciling spouses, though the verse addresses real estrangement.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A soft answer turneth away wrath; but a grievous word stirreth up anger.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that gentle words usually calm anger.
judaism.tie_back: The joke of the Kural is that the husband’s soft answer does not turn away his wife’s wrath, but stirs up a new sulk.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a contrastive match, since the Kural shows the usual rule failing in the game of love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges people to stop examining others for faults and look at themselves instead.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife keeps finding fault even in her husband’s kindness, the habit the verse asks us to drop.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a contrastive match only, since the Kural’s fault-finding is affectionate play.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching pictures desire and delusion as an endless loop, each producing the other.
jainism.tie_back: The wife’s sulking works like that loop: each reconciliation gives birth to a new sulk.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a next-best match on a self-renewing cycle, from a teaching aimed at escaping desire altogether.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, when Jupiter hides his love Io by turning her into a heifer, Juno is not soothed by his explanations but asks for the heifer as a gift and sets hundred-eyed Argus to guard her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Juno’s suspicion survives every attempt by her husband to smooth things over.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, will not let her husband’s soothing words put her suspicion to rest.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous tale; a partial match on suspicion that resists soothing, though Juno’s suspicion is justified.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy The Girl from Andros, an old man says that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love (amantium irae amoris integratio est).
philosophy.explanation: The line, from Roman comic drama rather than philosophy proper, became a proverb for the idea that lovers’ quarrels refresh love.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the spirit of the whole chapter: the wife’s endless mock quarrels keep love lively.
philosophy.source: Terence, Andria 555 (paraphrase of a proverbial line)
philosophy._accuracy_note: A famous proverbial line from Roman comedy, given here as a paraphrase; a strong thematic match, though Terence is a dramatist, not a philosopher.

kurals.tamil:
நினைத்திருந்து நோக்கினும் காயும் அனைத்துநீர்
யாருள்ளி நோக்கினீர் என்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Ninaiththirundhu noakkinum kaayum anaiththu-neer
yaarulli noakkineer endru
kurals.meaning: Even when I sit quietly gazing at her, lost in thoughts of her beauty, she grows angry: ‘Whom are you thinking of as you look me over?’
kurals.elementary: Imagine staring happily at your favourite painting, and your sister asks, ‘Are you comparing it to some other painting?’ The husband just wants to admire his wife, but she pretends he must be comparing her to someone else.
kurals.university: Niṉaittiruntu nōkkiṉum means ‘even if I look, having (silently) contemplated’, i.e. gazing at her while dwelling on her beauty; she grows hot (kāyum) and asks yār uḷḷi nōkkiṉīr (‘with whom in mind did you look?’). Aṉaittum is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘all (her features) by comparison’ (ollumaiyāka ellām) and by Solomon Pappaiah as gazing at each of her features, which she takes as matching them against another woman’s. As the chapter’s last couplet it caps the series: speech (1314-1316), sneezing (1317-1318), coaxing (1319), and finally even silent admiration all provoke pulavi. Pope: ‘I silent sat, but thought the more, and gazed on her. Then she cried out, “While thus you eye me o’er, tell me whose form you see.”’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna teases his devoted wife Rukmini by asking why she chose him over more suitable kings; she takes his playful words seriously and is overcome, and he must comfort her.
hinduism.explanation: The scene shows a loving wife reading hurt into her husband’s light-hearted attention.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise reads a slight into her husband’s loving gaze, though here he meant no teasing at all.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; a partial match on a wife misreading loving attention, though Krishna’s words were deliberately teasing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs gazes on his beloved and finds her wholly beautiful, with no comparison to anyone.
christianity.tie_back: This is what the husband is thinking as he gazes, even while his wife pretends he is comparing her to another.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on admiring gaze, though the Song lacks the wife’s teasing reply.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an presents spouses as a source of peace and affection for each other.
islam.tie_back: The husband’s quiet gaze is that tranquil affection; the wife’s mock anger is only a playful ripple on it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a general match on marital affection, not on jealousy or gazing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My dove, my undefiled, is but one; she is the only one of her mother; she is the choice one of her that bore her.”
judaism.explanation: Surrounded by queens and maidens without number, the lover insists that his beloved is the only one.
judaism.tie_back: The husband’s gaze means just this: there is no one else he is measuring her against.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org; a good match answering the wife’s ‘whom are you comparing me to?’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhariya Sutta, the Buddha describes seven kinds of wives, among them the ‘friend-wife’, who rejoices on seeing her husband as one friend rejoices at seeing another after a long time.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha holds up a marriage where seeing each other brings simple gladness.
buddhism.tie_back: The husband’s loving gaze invites that gladness, though his wife, in play, answers with suspicion instead.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; a partial match on gladness in seeing a spouse, with no jealousy theme.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who passionately hates (a colour), will at the same moment suffer pain. It is the fault of an undisciplined man that he is annoyed (by a colour); it is not the ‘colour’ itself that annoys him.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching places the source of annoyance in the mind of the one annoyed, not in the thing seen.
jainism.tie_back: Nothing in the husband’s gaze is wrong; any annoyance is created by the wife’s own playful mind.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi); a partial match on annoyance arising in the mind, from a teaching on detachment rather than love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho’s famous poem describes watching the man who sits close to her beloved and listens to her sweet voice, and the overwhelming tumult the sight stirs in the watcher.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poem is antiquity’s classic portrait of gazing, love and jealous turmoil all at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural joins the same elements: a loving gaze and an imagined third person stirring jealousy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous lyric; a partial match on gaze and jealousy, though Sappho is a lyric poet rather than a myth and her poem’s situation differs.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates describes the lover who, gazing on the beauty of the beloved, is filled with awe and warmth and wants only to keep looking.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats the lover’s gaze as a wholehearted response to the beauty in front of him.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the husband’s silent gaze in the Kural, wholly fixed on his wife, though she teasingly suspects otherwise.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a fair match on the lover’s rapt gaze, though Plato’s purpose is philosophical.
